title: Robin's Happy Mix-Up
markdown:
In days long vanished only as far as last autumn’s leaf-mould, Robin the weasel smoothed his tweed waistcoat and regarded the Grand Botanical Glasshouse as a promise he intended to keep. Tonight was the annual membership supper. Robin knew this place better than the tunnels under his burrow. Every label mattered. The elderflower cordial had to sit at the right temperature. Planning, he believed, was a strong vine for happiness to grow on.

“Are you sure about where the Himalayan Blue Poppies are, Robin?” asked Bea the goat. Her voice was a soft bleat that always made him pause. She perched on a wooden stool, dusting a fern. Feathers floated like tiny snow. Bea was Robin’s flatmate, calm and kind, and sometimes a little messy, which made her a good balance to his careful ideas. “They look a bit lonely there. Like they’re floating in all that green.”

Robin sighed, a sound like rustling leaves. “Bea, my dear, their spot is on purpose. It shows how special they are. We are not losing control. We are showing their uniqueness. It is about seeing their specialness, not hiding it in a crowd.”

He looked around and felt a quiet happiness. Lanterns glowed. The air smelled of earth and flowers. In the glasshouse panes the lanterns doubled themselves, a first trembling reflection of the evening he had arranged. He had made programmes for everyone, tied with neat red ribbons. He patted the stack. It wobbled. The ribbons seemed to protest. He fixed it quickly. His whiskers twitched just a little.

Just as he thought about opening the elderflower cider, the big glass doors opened with a sweep. First came the members of the Illustrious Orchid Society, velvet clothes and shiny brooches, smiling at the orchids Robin had placed to catch the light. They arrived exactly as the programme promised, and Robin’s vine of a plan seemed, for a moment, to have flowered on cue.

Before Robin could say hello, the doors opened again. The Enthusiastic Fern Fanatics walked in, sturdy boots and small trowels, heading straight for the shady damp spots. They spoke in quiet voices about the delicate fronds of the tree ferns. Already each group believed itself the only honoured party.

Then the doors burst open with a playful push. The Bold Bromeliad Brigade arrived in bright Hawaiian shirts and wide hats, laughing, their sharp eyes finding the bromeliads at once. A happy chorus rose. Three exclusive invitations, granted by the same open door.

Robin blinked. His weasel eyes widened. Bea looked over her stool. “Oh dear,” she bleated softly. “That seems like a lot of honoured guests for one supper. It’s quite a crowd.”

Robin’s whiskers twitched. He imagined his nice evening turning into a jumble of plant talk. Then he looked at Bea. She was already offering a tray of small acorn-shaped biscuits to a surprised orchid guest. She was not worried. She was being kind. Her calm was stronger than his strict plan.

He took a deep breath. The air smelled of earth and flowers. In a nearby pane he caught his own face, a second reflection, looking rather tighter than a host ought to look. “Bea,” he said, his voice steady, “maybe our idea of supper needs to be a little wider. A bit more flexible.”

Bea’s eyes twinkled. She spoke as if the glasshouse itself had lent her a couplet.

“Share the glasshouse, share the vine.
Joy grows wider than the line.”

He straightened his waistcoat and walked to the guests. The Orchid Society was looking closely at a beautiful flower. The Fern Fanatics were talking about how plants grow. The Bromeliad Brigade was pointing out bright colours and interesting leaves. They were not being mean. They were enjoying their own favourite plants.

“Welcome, everyone,” Robin said, his voice clear across the big room. “I am Robin, the garden historian. It seems there was a small mix-up with the invitations. It was not part of my plan.” A few friendly chuckles rose. “But sometimes the best discoveries happen when we least expect them. This glasshouse is a place of wonder. Tonight it may also be a place for unexpected friendship.”

He saw Bea wink, still holding a biscuit. He looked at the stack of programmes. The ribbons no longer seemed rebellious. They looked like an invitation. His idea of joy had been too small, too tight.

“Instead of separate tours,” he said, warmer now, “why don’t we explore this place together? Why don’t we share what we love? The orchids, the ferns, the bromeliads all speak the same language of nature. A language of strength, of cleverness, and of quiet beauty.”

Slowly at first, then with more confidence, the groups began to talk. Orchid members discussed plant shapes with the Fern Fanatics. The Bromeliad Brigade shared growing tips and learned the soft beauty of orchid petals. Bea walked her tray, making sure everyone had a biscuit and a friendly word.

By the time the elderflower cordial was poured, a real warmth filled the glasshouse. In each glass the elderflower trembled like a small lake, a third reflection, no longer a private supper but a shared one. Laughter, not polite but happy, echoed in the air. The evening had lost its stiffness and gained a comfortable feeling of enjoyment. As the last guests left, promising to visit again, Robin turned to Bea.

What he had wanted inverted itself. He had asked for one society, one programme, one vine trained to a single wall. The glasshouse had given him three societies and room enough to hold them all.

Bea was already tidying fallen leaves and biscuit crumbs. She bleated happily. Her eyes twinkled in the lantern light. Robin smiled a real smile, and the panes kept the lanterns a little longer, as if the glasshouse, having granted more than he asked, was content to keep the extra light.
characters: Robin (weasel garden historian in a tweed waistcoat), Bea (a goat flatmate of feather-duster calm)
